1:
Who these elders were is disputed. Gill reports the view of Kimchi that they were heads of the captives already in Babylon, but notes that others take them for men come from Jerusalem who called on the prophet. Henry prefers the second: they were not his fellow captives but occasional hearers, grandees of the city come to Babylon perhaps on an embassy, who turned aside on the way. Keil and Delitzsch reject that, holding them to be elders of the exiles among whom the prophet had been labouring; and Ellicott closes the question from the wording, since no distinction is intended between the elders of Israel here and the elders of Judah named earlier.

Their motive is read darkly. Henry suspects a design to ensnare the prophet, or to catch at anything that might look like a contradiction to what Jeremiah had prophesied; yet they feigned themselves just men and sat before him as gravely as the people of God used to sit, from which he notes that it is no new thing for bad men to be employed in the external performances of religion. Clarke thinks they came to tempt him, or to get him to say something that would embroil him with the government. Calvin reads the posture as the sign of anxiety and despair that men show when evils perplex them and they see no remedy. He allows that the prophet might well have been touched and softened; and that is exactly why the warning came in time, God instructing his servant not to give way too easily when he sees old men coming to be disciples.

Ellicott says what was uppermost in their minds, and it governs the chapter. Told already that the city would not be spared for its own sake, and that long forbearance was no warrant for more, they still cherished the hope that however sinful they were it would be delivered for the sake of the holy men living in it. Keil and Delitzsch set out the same architecture, two words of God: the first refusing the idolater any answer and threatening the prophet who ventures one, the second denouncing the hope that the place would be spared for the righteousness of the godly within it. Clarke lists the four judgments to follow, famine, wild beasts, sword and pestilence.

On idols set up in the heart the treatments sharpen. Gill observes that they are far from home and have no images with them, and yet carry them in fancy, so that their hearts are the altars on which they worship and the throne on which they have placed them; he turns the point by asking what else a man own righteousness is when it is made an idol and trusted in. Calvin finds an implied comparison between God and the idol. God has erected the seat of his empire in our hearts, so that whoever sets up an idol there attempts to overthrow that throne, which makes the charge sacrilege of the most heinous kind. Clarke says the idols were not only in their houses and in the streets but in their hearts; they fell over them and broke the neck of their souls.

Two voices resist making them gross idolaters. Ellicott holds that the open idolatry of the homeland is not what is reproved here, since that had passed away among the captives; their heart was not right, and like the wife of Lot they longed for what they dared not do. Keil and Delitzsch say the same on lexical grounds, the phrase meaning to let a thing come into the mind, to be mentally busy with it, so that these elders are not to be pictured as given over to idolatry outright. Wesley takes the harder line, calling them resolved idolaters and the stumbling block their idols, the object of their sin and the occasion of their ruin.
4:
The promise to answer such men is read as a threat. Ellicott begins with the grammar. The words that cometh are not in the original and should be dropped, and the verb is passive with a reflexive force, so that the sense is that God will show himself answering. He states the rest as a principle: when a man persists in going counter to a known will, he is allowed to misunderstand it, as happened with Balaam and Micaiah; no one can know what he ought to do unless his own heart is submissive. The threat is that a man who inquires with a heart full of idols will get no true answer, but will find himself deceived by the illusions of his own heart. Clarke says God will treat him as an idolater, and Wesley that the answer will come according to his desert and in just judgment.

Calvin faces the objection that this looks like indulgence, and answers by distinguishing two things. Prophecy is in itself an image of the paternal anxiety of God for our salvation; but sometimes an answer ends only in destruction, and where God answers as a judge and removes all hope of pardon, no taste of his favour can be perceived. What these men wanted was a flattering answer, being accustomed to lies and having itching ears which the false prophets had gratified; what they will find is the difference between God and Satan. They bring with them the material of their own condemnation, and will carry nothing away but the seal of a sentence already written on their hearts.

On being taken in their own heart the readings converge. Gill takes it as exposure, God answering by righteous judgments so as to draw the hypocrisy out of them and make it manifest to others. Calvin gives the same account with more heat. So long as God spares the impious they try to soothe him; when they see that their blandishments take nothing, they roar and bellow against him, and the dissembling is stripped away so that anyone may see there was never a spark of piety. The word of God is a two-edged sword that examines all the sentiments of men: some are so slain by it that they grow wise again, others are only stung into fury when they find they must contend with power. Wesley draws the general rule, that it is always through some idol that the hearts of men are estranged, some creature having gained the place that belongs to none but God.

The call to repent is what all this was for. Gill notes that the end of every threatening is to bring men to repentance, and Calvin makes it turn thus: when he inspires us with fear he intends nothing but to humble us and provide for our salvation, being verbally angry that he may really spare. Ellicott adds the qualification that no outward reformation will serve, since they have to do with the Searcher of hearts and the only repentance he accepts is one seated in the affections.

Calvin ends on a difficulty in the second verb. Some take the word to mean wives, which he calls frigid; others make it transitive but impersonal, so that the sense would be make yourselves return, which he calls harsh. He has no doubt each man is exhorted to reconcile himself to God and bring others back with him. Since many had been the authors of evil to one another, they are now to do their utmost to recover one another; and this is the true proof of repentance, that we are not converted one by one only but stretch out a hand to our brethren and recall them from error. Where they wandered away through our fault, the obligation is stronger still, and the injury must be made up by at least equal diligence.
7:
The extension of the threat to the stranger is explained two ways. Ellicott takes it legally: a resident foreigner was bound to an outward deference to the law of the land, and since this nation was a theocracy its fundamental law against idol worship could not be violated with impunity by anyone who sought the protection of its government. Calvin distinguishes two kinds of stranger. Some merely transacted business there and remained profane and uncircumcised; others, though not sprung from the sacred race, had been circumcised and so far as religion went were members of the church, and God will have these reckoned in the same rank as the sons of Abraham, the law being one for the stranger and the home born. But he then turns the inclusion into an aggravation. That a settler should embrace the law was in a sense accidental, whereas these were heirs by birth, the adoption running on through successive ages, so that their departure was the more disgraceful.

Ellicott states exactly what the hypocrisy consists in. Outward idolatry is not charged; the accusations refer only to a secret idolatry of the heart, and the point pressed is not the idol worship but the attempt to join with it the inquiring of the Lord. Hence the answer comes not through the prophet consulted but from God interposing directly to punish the inquirer and make him an example to deter others. Wesley puts the same thing: the man shall find by the answer that it was not the prophet but God who answered, so dreadful and searching will it be. Clarke notes that the prophet consulted is taken to be a false one, and observes the irony: while the false prophets assured them of peace and prosperity the true were predicting the calamities that afterwards fell, and they believed the false in preference. He illustrates it from the king who asked one prophet about the battle and was told he would lose it, then asked another who promised a glorious victory, marched, and was killed.

On God setting his face Gill and Calvin both reach for the language of confrontation. Gill has him look the man out of countenance for all his impudence in coming to inquire while guilty of idolatry, and notes that the Targum renders the phrase as fury, which he thinks the sense. Calvin makes the idiom more physical still: a man is said to set his face against another when he rises against him, or descends into the contest and engages hand to hand.

Calvin also explains why the effect is promised as well as the word. Profane men fabricate empty treaties for themselves, and when God threatens they say it is only thunder without lightning; God declares that they will perceive by the event how truly he had spoken. When God answers in himself he does not strike the air with words but denounces what he has determined to fulfil in his own time, never answering without joining the effect to the prophecy. The prophets are on this account heralds of a wrath already hanging over the men they address.

The last clause turns on a textual question. Ellicott holds the Hebrew text preferable to its margin, which both the translators and the ancient versions followed, and would render it that God will make the man desolate for a sign and a proverb; the English, he says, almost loses the idea of wonder the severity is meant to provoke. Calvin arrives at the same emphasis without the textual argument, distinguishing the ordinary chastisement of faults, inflicted after a common and accustomed manner, from a punishment that excites the wonder of everyone and stands like a portent, where God puts forth the sign of his wrath in no common fashion. Wesley reduces the whole to three words, that the sign is one of divine vengeance.
9:
The hardest sentence in the chapter is the one where God claims to have deceived the prophet. Clarke states a rule of language, that Hebrew commonly says a thing is done by the Lord which he only suffers or permits, the government of God being so absolute that nothing can occur without his permission. Wesley says it in a phrase, that God permitted him to err or justly left him in his blindness. Ellicott gives the fullest account. The exact sense is that if a prophet is persuaded and speaks a word, God has persuaded that prophet, and he persuades in the same way in which he hardened the heart of Pharaoh, by making such persuasion the natural consequence of ordained moral law. Men are held back from sin only by his own Spirit drawing them; where they set that aside, the tendency is toward further sin. God forces no one to receive truth, but where the heart is set on wrong he gives men up and sends a strong delusion. The man who refuses the medicine, he adds, must sink under the disease.

Calvin approaches it from the situation. The people had their own impostors to hand and treated them as a shield against every threat: two or three prophets take away our hope, they said, but others, far more of them, promise us security, so there is no need to despair. The answer God gives is that the flatterers themselves err through the fault of those who want to be flattered, and that he deceives them because such impiety deserves it.

That both parties bear the punishment is agreed. Clarke states it flatly, that both have left the Lord and both shall be equally punished. Gill dwells on what bearing it means, calling the case sad when a man must carry his own sins and their punishment with no surety to undertake for him. Calvin observes that when God calls himself a searcher of hearts, hypocrites who have only men to deal with delude them easily, but when God addresses them the language penetrates to their hidden thoughts.

Calvin also pauses over the title. He takes it as a concession of speech rather than a description, and admits the stumbling block it creates, since when the weak hear impostors boasting in that name they are disturbed, and not without reason, prophets being organs of the Spirit. God grants the word without granting the thing.

The purpose of the severity is stated at the end. Ellicott finds in it the object of every judgment, that this people should be brought to a true repentance and restored to communion. Gill notices that the punishment of some is among the means God uses to reclaim others. Calvin turns it into an answer to an objection: if both people and prophets are destined to destruction the covenant seems void, and he replies that the rigour itself is useful to the church, the obstinacy being otherwise incurable. He adds that those sons are incorrigible indeed who despise a father while he cherishes and indulges them, and grow worse by the indulgence. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both mark the hinge into what follows. The threat so far left open the possibility that God might spare the city for the sake of the righteous in it, as had been promised in the case of Sodom and Gomorrah; that hope is what the next oracle is written to remove. Ellicott sets out its shape in advance: a land sinning so grievously would not be spared though three named righteous men were in it, the point is repeated with each of four judgments, and the climax comes when all four are combined. He notes that Jeremiah had said much the same a few years earlier in a denunciation of false prophets, where even the presence of Moses and Samuel was declared unavailing.
12:
Gill begins by resisting a division. The formula that opens this section does not, in his view, begin a new prophecy but continues the same one at the same time, still denouncing judgments, and he notes that the Targum renders it simply the word of prophecy from the Lord. That runs against those who treat what follows as a distinct communication, and the difference matters for how tightly the four judgments are bound to the refusal of an answer that went before.

Henry states the governing principle in a phrase and then unfolds it. National sins bring national judgments; when virtue is ruined and laid waste everything else will soon be ruined and laid waste too. The land is said to sin when vice becomes epidemical, when the sinners have grown numerous and their sins heinous, and when gross impieties prevail universally; and then the divine power is openly exerted, the judgment stretched out to all the corners of the land and to all the concerns of the nation. Grievous sins, he says, bring grievous plagues. Gill makes the distinction more carefully, that these are not merely sinners as all men are but notorious ones, guilty of great prevarication and treachery; God is longsuffering, and does not usually come forth in judgment until sin has prevailed universally and is persisted in. Clarke says the same in a clause, that they had been frequently warned and refused to leave their sin, and so filled up the measure of their iniquity.

Ellicott approaches the verse as grammar with a consequence. The definite article is absent in the Hebrew and should be dropped, since the proposition is general and not a description of this land in particular; and for the same reason the futures ought to be rendered as presents, so that it reads as a standing rule about what happens when a land sins, God stretches out his hand, breaks the staff of bread, sends famine and cuts off man and beast. He adds that famine was among the judgments threatened in the warnings of the law, where the other woes named here stood in immediate connection with it.

Henry draws a second principle out of the fact that four judgments are named rather than one. God has a variety of sore judgments with which to punish a sinful nation, has them all at command, and inflicts which he pleases. He recalls that a king who had sinned in numbering the people was given his choice of which judgment should fall, since any would answer the end of lessening the numbers he had been proud of; and that the king in effect handed the choice back, saying let us fall into the hands of the Lord and let him choose with what rod we shall be beaten. The reason God uses a variety, Henry suggests, is that it may appear he has universal dominion, and that in all our concerns we may see our dependence on him.

On the first of the four Henry is most compressed. The denying of common mercies is itself judgment enough, and there needs no more to make a people miserable; God has no need to bring the staff of oppression, since it is only breaking the staff of bread and the work is soon done. He cuts off man and beast together by cutting off the provision that nature makes for both in the annual products of the earth. Calvin adds a point of construction that governs the sequence: some interpreters pervert the sense by ending the sentence at the stretching out of the hand, as though that were the whole threat, whereas the clause is dependent and runs on. The threat is not simply that judgment comes, but that the presence of righteous men within the land will not turn it aside, which is what the rest of the chapter exists to establish.
14:
Why these three names and no others is answered the same way by four voices. Ellicott holds they were chosen not only as examples of holiness but as men allowed to be the means of saving others: for the sake of Noah his whole family was spared, Daniel was the means of saving his companions, and the friends of Job were spared through his intercession. He notes that Moses and Samuel might seem still more remarkable instances, but that Jeremiah had already used them. Gill adds that these were men eminent for prayer and successful in it, and Wesley that Noah prevailed to have the world spared for some years, that Daniel prevailed for the life of the wise men of Chaldea, and that Job offered sacrifice daily for his children.

Clarke argues from the opposite end, that the intercession even of the holiest shall not avert judgment, and finds a limit in each of the three careers. Noah could not by intercession keep the old world from being drowned; Job could not preserve his children from being killed by the fall of their house; Daniel could not prevent the captivity of his country. He draws two conclusions: that where God has determined to punish a nation no intercession will avail, personal holiness availing only for the man who has it; and that from being named in this company we may infer Job was as real a person as the other two, of whose identity no one has pretended to doubt.

The presence of a living contemporary among two ancient figures raises a question, and Ellicott meets it at length. He sees no cause for surprise, since the distance between Noah and Job was greater than that between Job and Daniel, and a contemporary was needed to bring out the thought that the holiest men of past or present alike would avail nothing. He observes too that Daniel was separated from Ezekiel by circumstance as much as from the patriarchs by time, the one a captive among captives and the other in high office at the royal court. He therefore rejects the strange supposition that some older Daniel is meant, a man eminent enough to be named here and yet whose name has otherwise faded out of history. He adds what he thinks the decisive propriety: Daniel was the trusted counsellor of the king by whom the city was to be destroyed, so that people might well have supposed his influence would avert the calamity. Clarke reaches the same identification by chronology, reckoning from the year of the captivity and the lengths of the intervening reigns that Daniel had been fourteen years in exile, and had already gained much public celebrity; Ellicott puts the interval at about twelve.

Gill and Calvin are concerned with why the intercession fails. Gill says the decree had gone forth and was not to be called in, being unalterable and God inexorable. Calvin faces the contradiction between a God elsewhere promising mercy and one here leaving no hope of pardon. His answer is the distinction he has used throughout, that the prophets sometimes address the body of the people, by then like a putrid carcass, and afterwards moderate that rigour when they turn to the remnant, so that the covenant is not extinguished. Where we meet this kind of contradiction, the rule is that no hope is afforded the reprobate, while any interspersed testimony of favour is meant for the church and its surviving seed.

Calvin then cites the parallel where Jeremiah was told that though Moses and Samuel stood before him God would not turn toward this people, and denies a use that has been made of it. The passage cannot show that the dead intercede for the living, since the construction is hypothetical: the point is that even if such men should pray, the prayers would not be granted.
15:
Calvin treats the four scourges as a recognised set, hunger and wild beasts, war and pestilence, and notes that the second is the one Scripture uses least, the beasts appearing only where the scourges are treated distinctly. His argument is that they do not break in by chance. God carries out his judgments no less by lions and bears than by rain and drought and the sword: these creatures are hostile to the human race and would tear in pieces everyone they met, were they not held back by a secret instinct from God. If he restrains them, he also lets them loose as often as it pleases him. Gill takes the beasts as pernicious rather than poisonous, lions and foxes and wolves and bears, especially ravenous after a famine.

The oath sworn over the second judgment draws a note from Calvin, that God swears by his own life, since he has no greater by whom to swear. Gill answers the objection about the three names, that two were not then among the living and the third was in Babylon; but had all three stood in such a land it would still have been in vain.

On the sword Calvin makes his sharpest claim. We think wars are stirred up at random: men are enraged, their swords fly about in their hands, and they seem to go this way and that by blind impulse. But God governs even wars by his own wisdom, and men and their swords with them. It would not be very wonderful, he says, if the text merely said that God would arm men; the prophet goes further, saying that the swords themselves listen to a secret command, so that they neither pass by nor strike any man or beast except so far as God pleases. From this he draws the rule that when men rise against us our patience is exercised and our sins chastised, and that we shall never profit by noise and resistance, there being one remedy only, to humble ourselves.

On the fourth Calvin notices a change of number. Earlier it was said that the three would not free either sons or daughters; now the singular is used, so that they should not prevail to save so much as one son or one daughter. He adds a limit to what is being taught. God does not always act as the passage describes, having manifold methods of carrying out his judgments, and it would not be right to impose on him a law never to deliver anyone; the point here is only that where he has determined to destroy a land there is no hope of pardon. Wesley glosses the fourth as death and destruction, not by the sword.

The last verse is the climax, an argument from the less to the greater. Ellicott says the teaching of the preceding verses is here gathered up: if the presence of the holiest would not avert any one of the four, how much more impossible to stay the doom when all four fall together. Wesley puts it that those who could not keep off one would be far less able to keep off all four commissioned to go at once, and Calvin as a picture, of four armies drawn up and ordered to attack. Calvin adds what the argument was aimed at, the specious hopes by which false prophets had deluded the exiles, promising a return. Clarke supplies definitions for the four, war for the sword, drought behind the famine, epidemic disease for the pestilence, and for the beasts their multiplication following on the general destruction of the inhabitants. Calvin ends on the word evil, taken in the sense in which God elsewhere says he creates good and evil; what is against us is called evil by reference to our own perception, since common sense calls good whatever is useful to us.
22:
The remnant left after the four judgments is where the commentators divide, and the division is about whether it is mercy at all. Gill reads it as wonder. In a land visited by a single judgment there was no escape, not so much as a son or daughter delivered; yet here, where all four fall together, a remnant is saved, and because that is beyond expectation the clause opens with a word at once a note of attention and of admiration. Calvin sets himself against that reading. Almost all, he grants, explain the verse parenthetically, as though God were correcting himself and engaging to deal more mercifully with this city; but weighing the intention more accurately he cannot subscribe to it, and takes the verse as confirming what went before, that God is a just avenger even in treating them so harshly.

His argument turns on what exile was. The condition of these men was worse than being destroyed by a single death, since they were dying daily, and once cast out of the holy land they were as good as dead. Those who died quickly, he says, were the less to be deplored. On that reckoning being brought out alive is no mitigation, and when the prophet says some will come to Babylon he is not promising pardon, since he speaks of men who carried the sign of their impiety on their foreheads.

Ellicott settles the harder question, what the comfort consists in, and holds that the connection decides it. The following clause explains why the sight of them helps: when you see their ways and their doings you will know that nothing has been done without cause. That is, when you see the wickedness of these survivors you will stop mourning over the judgment, because you cannot help perceiving it to have been a righteous act. He adds a point of idiom, that the phrase in the last verse means not that they will administer comfort but that they will be a cause of it, and that by showing their exceeding wickedness. Clarke reads it the same way, that their account of the abominations of the people will prove to those already in captivity with what propriety he acted.

Gill offers two ways of taking it, either that the survivors bring acknowledgment of their sins and repentance, or that the sight of their dissolute manner of life composes the minds of the exiles, satisfied that the judgment was just and that they were punished less than their sins deserved. Wesley takes the second, that they will be comforted when they compare the case of the newcomers with their own; and he draws out both halves of the reconciliation, to the justice of God in punishing his own people and to his goodness.

Calvin ends on the psychology of it. The consolation lies in the exiles acknowledging that cruelty cannot be charged on God, since the desperate wickedness of the people demanded what was done. From that he generalises: we are never tranquil in mind except where the greatest equity appears in the judgments of God, and so long as we do not acknowledge him to be severe in just causes our minds must be disturbed. The word consolation, he observes, is set against those turbulent thoughts. Since nothing is more miserable than to be drawn this way and that in anxiety, he concludes that those profit most who acquiesce in the judgments of God without perceiving the reason of them, and that when God does show why he has dealt so severely it is a special favour. Clarke reaches the same place by another road, that no part of the conduct of God toward men is dictated by anything but the purest principles of justice, equity and truth; in his justice there is no severity and in his mercy no caprice, and he alone does all things well.
